1.pericope_label: Listen, O isles, unto me: the Lord hath called me from the womb; and he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth

schools.summary: Treats the Servant as a figure held in tension with the nation, at once identified with Israel in fulfilling its ideal and distinguished from it as its Redeemer, and works the disputed clause about Israel's gathering as a matter of text rather than of consolation.
Sets aside the readings that make the speaker the conqueror or the prophet and hears Christ addressing the distant nations directly.
Reads the passage of Christ throughout while attending closely to the wording, one voice pressing the manuscripts and the classical parallels and the other paraphrasing the sense line by line.
Draws the whole out as encouragement for ministers who labour without visible fruit, and reads the Servant as the representative in whom all Israel is summed up.

debates.question: Who is the speaker of this chapter?

positions.view: Christ, and not the conqueror of Babylon nor the prophet himself, as earlier interpreters variously supposed
the mysterious Servant, at once identified with Israel in fulfilling its ideal and distinguished from it as its Restorer and Redeemer

the term contracts from its widest circumference, all Israel, to the true people within the nation, to its very centre, so that the speaker is the heart of Israel from which salvation flows to the nations
possibly the prophet, the conqueror, and the Messiah by turns, the earlier shadowing out the later, whatever the older expositors have proved; the literal sense should be sought first

debates.question: Does the negative in the clause about Israel not being gathered stand?

positions.view: no: manuscripts and the marginal correction read to him rather than not, and several versions drop the negative altogether
yes, and the clause states the failure under which the Servant is then comforted

outliers.reading: Alone leaves the Bible to defend the metaphor of speech as a weapon, quoting the comic poet on the sting Pericles left in his hearers and the lyric poet's habit of calling his own verses shafts, and judging the figure bold but just.
Would render the clause about glory as in whom I will glorify myself, making the Servant the means of a divine self-manifestation rather than merely its occasion.

themes: Listen, O isles, unto me; and hearken, ye people, from far; The Lord hath called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother hath he made mention of my name.
And he hath made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand hath he hid me, and made me a polished shaft; in his quiver hath he hid me;
And said unto me, Thou art my servant, O Israel, in whom I will be glorified.
Then I said, I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nought, and in vain: yet surely my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God.

And now, saith the Lord that formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob again to him, Though Israel be not gathered, yet shall I be glorious in the eyes of the Lord, and my God shall be my strength.

And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth.

7.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord, the Redeemer of Israel, to him whom man despiseth: kings shall see and arise; I will give thee for a covenant of the people, that thou mayest say to the prisoners, Go forth

schools.summary: Keeps the immediate reference to Israel while allowing a wider application, gives the literal senses of the season of good pleasure and of contempt reaching the soul, and canvasses the geography of the furthest land named.
Assigns the titles to the Father and the address to Christ, and reads the prison and the pastures throughout as figures of spiritual bondage and spiritual provision.
Divides between close textual criticism of the Hebrew and versions on one side and plain paraphrase on the other, both applying the release to the Gentiles.
Expounds the humiliation and exaltation together, makes the covenant clause the centre of the passage, and draws out the journey home as a pastoral figure of grace leading the redeemed to their rest.

debates.question: Where is the land of Sinim?

positions.view: the furthest edge of the prophet's horizon, and almost certainly the Chinese, known by name through ancient commerce
either the Sinites or the Egyptian Sin, standing for Egypt and so for the southern parts
probably a province of Babylon not elsewhere named in scripture
a woodland, from a root meaning bush; whence the question whether the lost tribes are not among the peoples of Africa and America whom Europeans think they have a right to enslave

debates.question: How far is the release of the prisoners a spiritual deliverance?

positions.view: wholly so: the prison is sin, the law, and Satan, and the prisoners are the Gentiles bound by the cords of their sins
the deliverance of Israel is the more prominent here, the immediate circle, though the words plainly have a wider and higher application

outliers.reading: Identifies the word for heat with the term used elsewhere of parched ground, so that what the pilgrims are shielded from is the mirage of the scorching desert rather than the sun's heat simply.

Works these verses as a textual critic where the others preach: a letter lost before his Holy One because the preceding word ended in the same consonant, a participle that should stand in the passive form, and a conjunction supplied by the manuscripts at the summons to those in darkness.

themes: Thus saith the Lord, the Redeemer of Israel, and his Holy One, to him whom man despiseth, to him whom the nation abhorreth, to a servant of rulers, Kings shall see and arise, princes also shall worship, because of the Lord that is faithful, and the Holy One of Israel, and he shall choose thee.

Thus saith the Lord, In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in a day of salvation have I helped thee: and I will preserve thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, to establish the earth, to cause to inherit the desolate heritages;
That thou mayest say to the prisoners, Go forth; to them that are in darkness, Shew yourselves. They shall feed in the ways, and their pastures shall be in all high places.
They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun smite them: for he that hath mercy on them shall lead them, even by the springs of water shall he guide them.
And I will make all my mountains a way, and my highways shall be exalted.
Behold, these shall come from far: and, lo, these from the north and from the west; and these from the land of Sinim.
Sing, O heavens; and be joyful, O earth; and break forth into singing, O mountains: for the Lord hath comforted his people, and will have mercy upon his afflicted.

14.pericope_label: But Zion said, The Lord hath forsaken me: can a woman forget her sucking child? Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me

schools.summary: Reads Zion's complaint as the church's failure of faith at the very moment of deliverance, gives the literal force of the bereavement and the too-narrow place, and weighs the ancient variant that turns her children into her builders.
Takes Zion for the church under the gospel throughout, and resists both the older Jewish gloss on the engraving and the customary identification of the lost children with the rejected Jews.
Presses the manuscripts hard on three separate readings while keeping the plain application, that the Gentiles are the children born to Zion when her natural children were cut off.
Argues the maternal comparison in two movements and prefers homely domestic tokens of remembrance to any exotic custom.

debates.question: What custom lies behind the engraving upon the palms of the hands?

positions.view: a real practice of marking the skin, punctures made indelible by fire or staining and bearing some sign of the city or the temple, as pilgrims are still marked
not that, and certainly not palmistry, but the homely tokens of remembrance, a string tied on the finger or a keepsake ring worn for an absent friend

debates.question: Should thy children be read thy builders?

positions.view: yes, on the authority of the ancient versions and a Talmudic direction; and further, the parallel clause should then say that the destroyers become her offspring, since the usual rendering is flat after their zeal has just been described
yes for the reading, but the destroyers still go forth while the builders rush to their work of restoration
the antithesis favours builders, yet sons suits what follows better, and the thought of children rebuilding the walls follows from the antithesis anyway
sons: the young converts who flock to the church

debates.question: Who are the children Zion lost, and who are those she gains?

positions.view: the Jews cut off by their own unbelief, and the Gentiles who came in their room
not those at all, but those destroyed by heathen persecution and antichristian cruelty, and the converts gathered when antichrist falls
simply the children of her bereavement, born while she thought herself bereaved

outliers.reading: Compares Zion gazing on her returning children with the mother who pointed to her sons as jewels better than a wealthy rival's gems.

Judges the clause about the bride defective, since a bride binds on ornaments and not children, and finds the lost word supplied in the Greek, the resemblance of the two Hebrew words having caused the omission.

themes: But Zion said, The Lord hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me.
Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.
Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me.
Thy children shall make haste; thy destroyers and they that made thee waste shall go forth of thee.

Lift up thine eyes round about, and behold: all these gather themselves together, and come to thee. As I live, saith the Lord, thou shalt surely clothe thee with them all, as with an ornament, and bind them on thee, as a bride doeth.
For thy waste and thy desolate places, and the land of thy destruction, shall even now be too narrow by reason of the inhabitants, and they that swallowed thee up shall be far away.
The children which thou shalt have, after thou hast lost the other, shall say again in thine ears, The place is too strait for me: give place to me that I may dwell.

Then shalt thou say in thine heart, Who hath begotten me these, seeing I have lost my children, and am desolate, a captive, and removing to and fro? and who hath brought up these? Behold, I was left alone; these, where had they been?

22.pericope_label: Behold, I will lift up mine hand to the Gentiles: and kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers; even the captives of the mighty shall be taken away

schools.summary: Keeps the imagery concrete, the signal raised for the nations and the royal fosterage that inverts ordinary court practice, and treats the sceptical question as a crux of text and of politics rather than of piety.
Refuses the figurative reading of the royal titles, names the monarchs in whom the promise was already part-fulfilled, and expects the mutual slaughter of the oppressors in a still future collapse.
Splits between a paraphrase that takes the homage at face value and a criticism that treats the prostration as oriental poetry and the disputed word as a copyist's error.
Reads the whole as promise and application together, naming the royal patrons of the church and turning the carrying of infants into a rule for handling young converts.

debates.question: Are the prostrating kings a prediction of literal homage?

positions.view: yes, and already part-fulfilled in named monarchs from the Persian court and a Jewish queen to the Christian emperors and their consorts, with a fuller accomplishment still to come
no: these are general poetical images drawn from the manners of the country, amplifications of the subject and not predictions to be fulfilled precisely according to the letter
real homage paid to the true Israel as the dwelling-place of God, the force of it lying in the inversion of a court custom by which kings gave their own children to nobles to rear
a standard against which governments are measured, since all that is true in the regal headship of the church will be realised here and all that is false in regal territorialism will condemn itself

debates.question: Should the captive of righteousness be emended to the captive of the terrible one?

positions.view: yes; the received reading is a palpable mistake, the correspondence between question and answer requires the change, and two versions support it
neither available sense is quite satisfactory, and the conjectural emendation fits the parallelism of the following verse
no; the parallelism does not compel it, the oppressor cannot be called righteous since he is wicked, and the phrase means no more than a host of captives belonging to the righteous
the difficulty is not textual at all: the captivity is lawful because the justice of God pleads against release, and the ransom is what answers it

outliers.reading: Assembles an anthology of eastern prostration behind the licking of the dust, the Persian court that admitted no one without the act of adoration, the Macedonians prostrating themselves before a king intoxicated with success, and a conquered prince who kissed the prints of his enemy's horse and made verses saying the mark in the dust served him now for a crown.
Denies that the eating of their own flesh means famine, and expects the mutual slaughter of the oppressors to be verified among the Popish party.

themes: Thus saith the Lord God, Behold, I will lift up mine hand to the Gentiles, and set up my standard to the people: and they shall bring thy sons in their arms, and thy daughters shall be carried upon their shoulders.

And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the Lord: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me.
Shall the prey be taken from the mighty, or the lawful captive delivered?

But thus saith the Lord, Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken away, and the prey of the terrible shall be delivered: for I will contend with him that contendeth with thee, and I will save thy children.

And I will feed them that oppress thee with their own flesh; and they shall be drunken with their own blood, as with sweet wine: and all flesh shall know that I the Lord am thy Saviour and thy Redeemer, the mighty One of Jacob.
